One of the earliest known references to the myth of the Great Wall's visibility from the Moon appears in a letter written in 1754 by the English antiquary [William Stukeley](/wiki/William_Stukeley "William Stukeley"). Stukeley wrote that, "This mighty wall [[Hadrian's Wall](/wiki/Hadrian%27s_Wall "Hadrian's Wall")] of four score miles [130 km] in length is only exceeded by the Chinese Wall, which makes a considerable figure upon the [terrestrial globe](/wiki/Terrestrial_globe "Terrestrial globe"), and may be discerned at the Moon."[[74]](#cite_note-74) The claim was also mentioned by [Henry Norman](/wiki/Sir_Henry_Norman,_1st_Baronet "Sir Henry Norman, 1st Baronet") in 1895, writing "besides its age it enjoys the reputation of being the only work of human hands on the globe visible from the Moon."[[75]](#cite_note-75) The myth also appears in the 1932 strip of *[Ripley's Believe It or Not!](/wiki/Ripley%27s_Believe_It_or_Not! "Ripley's Believe It or Not!").*[[76]](#cite_note-Ripley-76)
